summary: Describes how each new Unicode version must be reviewed for effects on Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA), and how the IETF decides between compatibility with older IDNA and with Unicode. It explains the role of the tables maintained for this purpose.

plainLanguage.summary: Whenever the alphabet of the whole world gets new letters, someone checks that website names written with them still work. This explains how that check is done.

questions: how does idna handle new unicode versions

subtitle: How each new Unicode version gets checked so internationalized domain names keep working.

tldr.problem: IDNA requires a review of every new Unicode version, but the requirement and the IANA tables tied to it were widely confused, and past reviews did not follow what RFC 5892 intended.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC splits the review into two parts, an algorithmic comparison of derived properties and an expert-team analysis of new code points, and restores the default of preserving the validity of existing labels.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 5892, makes clear that the IANA tables are not normative, and limits reviews to major Unicode versions unless something unusual arises.

sections.title: Why Unicode Versions Need Review
sections.content:
The standards for Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA) require a review of each new version of Unicode. The review looks for incompatibilities with earlier versions and, where needed, lets the IETF decide between compatibility with prior IDNA versions and compatibility with Unicode going forward.

That requirement, and its relationship to tables kept by IANA, has caused significant confusion. This document adjusts the review procedure based on nearly a decade of experience and updates RFC 5892. It does not change the duty of registries at every level of the DNS to take responsibility for the labels they insert, which means allowing only a subset of what IDNA itself permits.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing systems keep growing, so someone has to check that website names built from new letters still behave. This document explains how that check should work.

sections.title: IDNA2003, IDNA2008 and the Tables
sections.content:
The original IDNA, called IDNA2003, was defined using IETF-specific tables that were normative, so each table was tied to one Unicode version. As Unicode grew, a new profile would have been needed for every version.

The current version, IDNA2008, is property-based. Rules operate on Unicode properties to compute a derived property for each code point, and in principle they work with any Unicode version from about 5.0 forward. Because Unicode properties are not completely stable, IDNA2008 provided for an expert review of each new Unicode version, with possible exceptions to the rules. IANA keeps calculated tables for convenience, but those tables have never been normative. Statements that IDNA2008 is out of date because the IANA tables lag behind a Unicode version are incorrect or meaningless.
sections.plainLanguage: The old system was a fixed list that went stale. The new one is a set of rules that can be applied to any version of the alphabet list, with IANA keeping handy copies of the results.

sections.title: The Two-Part Review
sections.content:
IDNA2008 actually calls for two kinds of review when a new Unicode version appears. Unless the IESG or the expert team sees special problems, reviews are done only for major versions (numbered NN.0, such as 12.0), not minor ones (such as 12.1).

  • Part I, algorithmic comparison: compare derived properties computed from the new version with those from the previous one to find incompatible changes. Only one such review was completed under RFC 5892, for Unicode 6.0 (RFC 6452), which found three incompatibilities and chose to follow Unicode rather than preserve IDNA compatibility.
  • Part II, new code point analysis: review newly assigned code points to see whether they need special treatment, such as contextual rules, or break the assumptions behind the derived property calculations.

Part II must be done by a designated expert (DE) team, because no single expert is likely to have all the needed knowledge. The team should keep close contact with the Area Directors and have its membership reexamined at least annually. If Part II finds a problem, the affected code points are marked 'under review' in the IANA tables, should be considered unsafe, and are resolved later by IETF consensus.
sections.plainLanguage: One check compares the old and new lists to spot changes. The other check has a team of experts look at brand-new letters for tricky cases. Uncertain letters get a warning label until everyone agrees.

sections.title: Compatibility Versus Unicode
sections.content:
When IDNA2008 was written, the assumption was that incompatible Unicode changes would be handled by adding exceptions to preserve backward compatibility. The reviews for Unicode 6.0, 11.0 and 12.0 instead chose consistency with Unicode, which went against RFC 5892 and against commitments that valid labels would stay valid and invalid labels would stay invalid.

This RFC restores the original intent. Absent extremely strong evidence, on a per-code point basis, that preserving a label's status would cause significant harm, Unicode changes that affect derived properties are to be reflected in IDNA exceptions that preserve that status. For changes after Unicode 12.0, any such decision must be captured in a document expected to be a Standards Track RFC so the IETF can review it and keep a record.

One partial exception: code points flagged by the new code point analysis should be treated as unsafe and used only with extreme caution until the analysis concludes.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule is now: if a website name worked before, it should keep working, unless there is a really strong reason to change. New letters that experts are still worried about should be used carefully.

sections.title: The IANA Tables and Expert Roles
sections.content:
Because most IANA registries are authoritative, the IDNA tables registry led people to wrongly assume that missing tables for Unicode versions after 6.0 meant IDNA could not be used with later versions. IANA has now marked the tables as non-normative and retitled the registry from 'IDNA Parameters' to 'IDNA Rules and Derived Property Values'. If these changes do not reduce the confusion, the RFC says serious consideration should be given to eliminating the tables entirely.

For Part I, the IESG appoints a designated expert to produce derived property tables for IANA. For Part II, it appoints an expert team. Coordination with the IAB-appointed liaison to the Unicode Consortium is called essential, although one person no longer has to fill every role. The list of code points needing contextual rules, and those rules, remain normative.
sections.plainLanguage: The tables are a handy cheat sheet, not the official rulebook. IANA now labels them that way so nobody mistakes them for the law.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 5892
sections.content:
The RFC effectively replaces Section 5.1 of RFC 5892. The main changes are splitting the review into two parts that can finish at different times, specifying an expert team rather than a single expert, adding a Status field to the IANA tables so uncertain code points can be flagged without delaying use of a new Unicode version, and restricting reviews to major Unicode versions.

It also makes an editorial fix based on Erratum 3312. In Appendix A of RFC 5892 a rule using a code point must be evaluated separately for every occurrence of that code point in the label, and each evaluation must be True. The Rule Set in Appendix A.1 is replaced with a version that tests the virama case and the joining-type pattern around \u200C.
sections.plainLanguage: It rewrites part of the older rulebook to make the steps clearer and fixes a small mistake that had been reported.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Following these procedures should reduce confusion about IDNA requirements. Past confusion gave openings for bad behavior, so the changes should improve security to at least a small extent.

The goal is to keep derived property values stable. If changes to the calculation are not taken into account, a code point could move from DISALLOWED to PVALID or the reverse. That can change how labels are interpreted in ways that confuse users and might enable attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: If a letter suddenly changes from allowed to banned, or the reverse, people can be confused or tricked. Careful checking prevents that.
